speaker: ALEX
text: Episode 1 starts before the workshop starts. Today is pre-workshop setup: GitHub account, Git, VS Code, and the screen reader pieces that make everything usable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the goal is not just "install a few things." It is to make sure the whole setup is ready enough that Day 1 can actually be about learning.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. If the tools are in place first, the rest of the workshop has room to breathe. We are going to separate Git from GitHub, set up the account, turn on 2FA, tune a few accessibility settings, and make sure the editor and screen reader work together.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And by the end, we want proof that the setup works end to end, not just a pile of unchecked boxes.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the right mindset.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What does someone need before Day 1 begins?

speaker: ALEX
text: First, the basics: a computer, a stable internet connection, and headphones if the room is busy or you want cleaner screen reader audio. On the software side, you need a GitHub account, a supported browser, a screen reader, Git, and Visual Studio Code.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the big idea is that there is a hardware layer, a browser layer, and a developer tools layer.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. And if you are using agents or advanced accessibility features later, you also want current versions of your tools. But for this episode, the important thing is simple: get the core setup done before the workshop begins.

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's start with the account. Create your GitHub account first if you do not already have one.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That means choosing a username too, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. And that username matters. It shows up in issues, pull requests, comments, and anywhere else you contribute. Pick something you can live with in public, because it becomes part of your GitHub identity.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What else happens during signup?

speaker: ALEX
text: You verify your email address, and you complete the human verification step GitHub uses during account creation. Then, after the account is made, you check your inbox for the verification email and confirm that address as well.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And 2FA is not optional.

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. Two-factor authentication is required. It means signing in needs a second proof beyond your password, like a push approval, an authenticator code, a security key, or a passkey. The reason is straightforward: if someone gets your password, 2FA still protects the account.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is the easiest way to think about it?

speaker: ALEX
text: A password is one lock. 2FA adds a second lock. That second lock is what makes the account fit for workshop use.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How should someone set up 2FA without getting lost?

speaker: ALEX
text: Go to GitHub settings, open the security section, and start two-factor authentication. GitHub will walk you through the options. For most people, the easiest path is the GitHub Mobile app or an authenticator app. If you already use a security key or passkey, that is even stronger.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should they keep in mind during setup?

speaker: ALEX
text: Recovery codes. Save them somewhere safe right away. If you ever lose your phone or key, those codes may be the only way back in. Also, it is smart to register more than one second factor so you do not end up locked out.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the workflow is not just "turn it on." It is "turn it on, save recovery, add backup."

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should they do about GitHub accessibility settings?

speaker: ALEX
text: Once signed in, adjust the settings that make GitHub easier to use with a screen reader and keyboard. The highest priority is disabling hovercards, because they can get in the way. Then enable link underlines, which makes links easier to identify. If you like keyboard shortcuts, check the character key shortcut setting too. And choose a theme that gives you comfortable contrast.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That sounds small, but it changes the feel of the site a lot.

speaker: ALEX
text: It does. The best accessibility settings are the ones that reduce friction before it starts.

speaker: ALEX
text: Next, update your profile. Add a profile picture if you can, choose a clear notification email, and make sure your account details are current.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Why does that matter in a workshop?

speaker: ALEX
text: Because maintainers and classmates need a reliable way to recognize you and reach you. A clean profile makes collaboration easier, especially when you start opening pull requests or commenting on shared work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about feature previews?

speaker: ALEX
text: Check GitHub feature preview settings too. Some features appear there before they become standard. You do not need every preview turned on, but it helps to know where that area lives in case a workshop step depends on it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So it is a "know where to look" skill, not a "turn everything on" skill.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now the screen reader and browser setup. If you are on Windows, NVDA or JAWS are both supported. If you are on macOS, VoiceOver is the default choice. The workshop is designed to work with all of them, so choose the one you already know best.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the browser?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use a modern browser like Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari on Mac with VoiceOver. The important part is consistency. Pick one browser, learn its navigation patterns, and keep it stable during the workshop.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should be configured first?

speaker: ALEX
text: For NVDA, make sure web browsing features are on and that you are comfortable moving by headings, links, and form fields. For JAWS, confirm the same basic web navigation habits. For VoiceOver, turn on Quick Nav if that helps you move quickly through pages.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the real goal is not a perfect setup screen. It is reliable navigation.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the whole point.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now install Git. Git is the version control system itself. GitHub is the website and service built around it. They are related, but they are not the same thing.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That distinction matters, because people often use the names like they mean the same job.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Git lives on your machine and tracks changes to files. GitHub hosts repositories and collaboration tools online.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do you install it?

speaker: ALEX
text: On Windows, download and install Git from the official Git site. On macOS, install Git through the Xcode Command Line Tools or the Git installer. On Linux, use your package manager. After that, open a terminal and verify it with `git --version`.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And that verification is the proof that the install actually landed.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Do not assume. Check.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What comes next after Git is installed?

speaker: ALEX
text: Configure your Git identity. Set `user.name` and `user.email` so your commits are labeled correctly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Why does that matter?

speaker: ALEX
text: Because Git uses that identity on your work. It helps your commits show up under the right name and email, and it keeps collaboration clean.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So this is not cosmetic. It is part of how your work is recorded.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now install Visual Studio Code, or VS Code. That is the recommended editor for the workshop.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What makes it the recommendation?

speaker: ALEX
text: It is widely used, it works well with GitHub workflows, and it has strong keyboard support. It also has a screen reader mode, which is why it fits this workshop so well.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How should someone enable that mode?

speaker: ALEX
text: Install VS Code, open it, and turn on screen reader support. You can do that with the keyboard shortcut or from the Command Palette. Once it is on, VS Code speaks and behaves more predictably with assistive tech.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is the part that makes the editor feel like a tool instead of an obstacle.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if someone wants to work in the browser instead?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use github.dev. It is the browser-based editor alternative. You can open it from a repository and edit directly in the browser without installing a desktop editor.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So it is a backup path, not the main recommendation.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. It is useful when you want a lightweight option or when a desktop setup is not available.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now let's verify the whole setup end to end.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Meaning: GitHub account is active, 2FA is on, Git is installed, VS Code is installed, and the screen reader can move through the interface.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the checklist. Then confirm Git sees your identity, confirm VS Code opens, confirm screen reader mode is enabled, and confirm you can sign in to GitHub from the browser.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if browser-based sign-in opens during a Git action, that is expected.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Git and VS Code can hand authentication off to GitHub in the browser. You approve the sign-in there, and the tool picks up the result.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the last check is not just "did it install," but "did the whole chain connect."

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. That is the difference between setup and readiness.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should someone remember after this episode?

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub is your online workspace, Git is your version history engine, and VS Code is your editor. Add 2FA, save recovery codes, tune your accessibility settings, and verify everything before the workshop starts.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is a lot less mysterious when it is framed as a working system.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the idea. Next episode, we start using those tools with confidence instead of just preparing them.
